claims.text: In-situ mechanical testing combined with real-time microstructural characterization can reveal active deformation mechanisms in FeNiCrMn.
FeNiCrMn activates dislocation slip under elevated-temperature, mildly corrosive mechanical loading.
FeNiCrMn activates deformation twinning under elevated-temperature, mildly corrosive mechanical loading.
Dislocation slip and twinning enhance both strength and ductility relative to room-temperature baseline tests.
The as-produced FeNiCrMn alloy has a single-phase solid-solution microstructure.
The FeNiCrMn alloy is produced by conventional alloy synthesis without Co.
High-resolution SEM or synchrotron X-ray diffraction can concurrently track microstructural evolution during tensile and compression testing.
The proposed elevated-temperature and simulated corrosive conditions are representative of aerospace, energy, and automotive service environments.
Mechanical loading causes the development and evolution of dislocation networks in FeNiCrMn.
Mechanical loading causes the development and evolution of deformation twins in FeNiCrMn.
Minor phase transformations may occur during mechanical loading of FeNiCrMn.
Dislocation glide relieves internal strain under service-relevant mechanical loading.
Deformation twinning relieves internal strain under service-relevant mechanical loading.
The combined operation of dislocation glide and twinning enhances plasticity without compromising high strength.
The emergence of dislocation and twin structures correlates with improved strength and ductility.
Elevated-temperature testing produces more deformation twins than room-temperature testing.
Dynamic changes in dislocation density at elevated temperature improve the mechanical performance of FeNiCrMn.
The proposed behavior may not persist under long-term cyclic loading or substantially different corrosive conditions.
